name: Orac and Game of Life
description: Please notice the unusual memory limit of this problem. Orac likes games. Recently he came up with the new game, " Game of Life ". You should play this game on a black and white grid with $$$n$$$ rows and $$$m$$$ columns. Each cell is either black or white. For each iteration of the game (the initial iteration is $$$0$$$), the color of each cell will change under the following rules: If there are no adjacent cells with the same color as this cell on the current iteration, the color of it on the next iteration will be the same. Otherwise, the color of the cell on the next iteration will be different. Two cells are adjacent if they have a mutual edge. Now Orac has set an initial situation, and he wants to know for the cell $$$(i,j)$$$ (in $$$i$$$-th row and $$$j$$$-th column), what will be its color at the iteration $$$p$$$. He may ask you these questions several times.
input_specification: The first line contains three integers $$$n,m,t\ (1\le n,m\le 1000, 1\le t\le 100\,000)$$$, representing the number of rows, columns, and the number of Orac queries. Each of the following $$$n$$$ lines contains a binary string of length $$$m$$$, the $$$j$$$-th character in $$$i$$$-th line represents the initial color of cell $$$(i,j)$$$. ' 0 ' stands for white, ' 1 ' stands for black. Each of the following $$$t$$$ lines contains three integers $$$i,j,p\ (1\le i\le n, 1\le j\le m, 1\le p\le 10^{18})$$$, representing a query from Orac.
output_specification: Print $$$t$$$ lines, in $$$i$$$-th line you should print the answer to the $$$i$$$-th query by Orac. If the color of this cell is black, you should print ' 1 '; otherwise, you should write ' 0 '.
approach_summary: Formulate the state transition graph with non-negative weights. Execute Dijkstra's algorithm with priority queue to find shortest paths in O((V + E) log V).

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1349C — Orac and Game of Life [168. Dijkstra's Algorithm]
topic_editorial.summary: Single-source shortest path using Dijkstra's algorithm.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Because all edge weights are non-negative, the shortest distance to the unvisited vertex with the minimum tentative distance is finalized and cannot be decreased by further transitions (greedy choice property).
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Graph Modeling
Construct an adjacency list with pairs $(v, w)$ for each directed or undirected edge from $u$ to $v$ with weight $w \ge 0$.

### Step 2: Distance Table Initialization
Initialize $dist[v] = \infty$ for all vertices, with $dist[\text{source}] = 0$.
Push $(0, \text{source})$ into a min-priority queue `std::priority_queue<pair<long long, int>, vector<pair<long long, int>>, greater<>>`.

### Step 3: Relaxation Loop
While the priority queue is not empty:
1. Pop $(d, u)$. If $d > dist[u]$, discard (stale entry).
2. For each neighbor $(v, w)$ of $u$:
   If $dist[u] + w < dist[v]$:
   $$dist[v] = dist[u] + w$$
   Push $(dist[v], v)$ into the priority queue.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((V + E) \log V)$
  Every vertex is extracted from the priority queue at most once. For every edge, we perform at most one priority queue push operation taking $\mathcal{O}(\log V)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(V + E)$
  Required for storing the adjacency list and the distance array.
